samples.text:
Millions of people use social media every day, and many of them use fake names. Some people believe that social media companies should check the real identity of every user. I agree with this idea because it can make the internet more safer.

The first reason is that when people are anonymous, they often behave badly. They write rude comments, bully other users and spread false information, because they know nobody can find them. If companies verify the identity of every user, people will think more carefully before they post something. For example, a student who bully his classmate online would stop if he knows that his real name is shown.

The second reason is that verification can reduce crimes on the internet. There are many fake accounts which are used to cheat people or to steal their money. Also, some adults create false profiles to contact children. If every account is connected to a real person, the police can find the criminals more easy and the users will feel more protected.

However, there are some disadvantages. Some users worry about their privacy, because they have to give their ID card or passport to a company. If the company is hacked, this information can be stolen. Moreover, in some countries people use fake names to criticise the government safely, and verification can put them in danger.

In conclusion, I agree that social media companies should verify the real identity of users because it can reduce bullying and online crime. However, the companies must keep the personal information safe and they should not show the real names to everyone.

samples.text:
Online abuse, scams and fake accounts have become serious problems on social media, leading some people to argue that platforms should be required to verify the real identity of every user. Although I understand the reasons for this proposal, I largely disagree with it, since the risks to privacy and free expression outweigh the likely benefits.

Supporters of mandatory verification believe it would make users more accountable. When people know that their posts can be traced back to them, they may be less likely to harass others or spread deliberate misinformation. Verification could also make it harder for criminals to create multiple fake accounts for fraud, and it would help authorities to identify offenders more quickly.

However, the evidence that real names improve behaviour are limited. Many people already post offensive content under their own names, which suggests that anonymity is not the only cause of online abuse. At the same time, requiring every user to upload identity documents would create huge databases of sensitive information, which could be targeted by hackers or misused by the companies themselves. A single data breach could expose the personal details of millions of people.

Anonymity also protects vulnerable groups. Whistle-blowers, victims of domestic abuse and people who live under authoritarian governments often rely on pseudonyms to speak freely without putting themselves in danger. For them, compulsory verification could mean choosing between silence and serious risk, which would be a significant loss for public debate.

A better approach would be for platforms to invest in faster moderation, to verify accounts only in specific cases, such as those used for advertising or selling products, and to cooperate with police when a crime is reported.

In conclusion, while identity checks might reduce some harmful behaviour, I do not believe they should be applied to every user. Targeted measures would protect people more effectively without sacrificing privacy and freedom of speech.

samples.text:
As concerns grow about online harassment, fraud and coordinated disinformation, the idea of obliging social media companies to verify the real identity of every user has gained considerable support. I agree that anonymity is sometimes abused, but I disagree with universal verification, which I believe would create serious new harms while doing relatively little to address the existing ones.

The appeal of the proposal is understandable. Anonymous accounts can be created in seconds, allowing individuals to harass others, operate networks of fake profiles or impersonate legitimate businesses with little fear of consequence. Linking every account to a verified person would, in theory, restore a degree of accountability and make it easier for victims and law enforcement to pursue those responsible.

In practice, however, the relationship between anonymity and misconduct is weaker than often assumed. A great deal of abusive content is posted openly under users' real names, indicating that social norms and platform design shape behaviour at least as much as identifiability does. Meanwhile, compelling billions of users to submit passports or identity cards would concentrate highly sensitive data in the hands of private companies, whose record in safeguarding personal information is far from reassuring. The consequences of a breach on that scale could be severe.

Equally significant is the value of anonymity to those with legitimate reasons to conceal their identity. Journalists' sources, employees exposing wrongdoing and political dissidents in repressive states often depend on pseudonyms to speak at all. For such users, mandatory verification would not merely be inconvenient; it could expose them to retaliation, with a chilling effect on precisely the kind of speech that open societies should protect.

More proportionate measures are available: verification for accounts that advertise, sell goods or reach very large audiences, stronger moderation, and swift cooperation with courts when unlawful conduct is reported.

In conclusion, universal identity checks would be a blunt instrument whose costs to privacy and freedom of expression outweigh its limited benefits.
